problem: Lightweight VLMs reason and decide poorly in socially complex navigation scenes, while large VLMs are too costly for onboard use. Existing KD works at the visual-feature or token level and lacks coordination between global semantics and token behaviour, and it becomes unstable when model capacities differ.
motivation: Social robot navigation needs scene semantics and social norms, but onboard memory and small datasets limit model size. The authors observe that two VLMs of different size trained jointly can improve each other, provided that learning rate and temperature are matched to their capability and capacity.
key_idea: Jointly train a learner and a guide VLM with a combined semantic-contrastive and distributional JS-divergence objective (GCO), using asymmetric learning rates (by SFT performance) and asymmetric temperatures (by model size) (AGO).
insight: Both GCO terms are needed: GSL alone gives 0.818/0.821 and DRL alone 0.832/0.722 (learner/guide), while combining them gives 0.908/0.857 on SNEI. Adding AGO lifts this to 0.968/0.914. Symmetric temperatures underperform or collapse, and the best setting is learner 3.0 / guide 2.0. Too large a DRL weight (0.8) collapses the guide to 0.737, so alignment strength must match capacity. Small learners can even surpass their larger guides ('capacity inversion').
method: Competitive group: two VLMs (Learner A, Guide B; homogeneous or heterogeneous, e.g. Qwen2.5-VL / Qwen3-VL, 2B-8B) are trained jointly on the same data.
GCO loss: L = 1.0*L_sup + 0.5*L_GSL + 0.4*L_DRL, where L_sup is autoregressive LM loss on both models.
Global Semantic Loss (GSL): learnable attention pooling of the hidden states into a global vector, projected and L2-normalised, then an InfoNCE loss between the two models' vectors (batch size 16).
Distributional Regularization Loss (DRL): Jensen-Shannon divergence between the full-vocabulary softmax distributions of the two models, with each KL term scaled by tau^2.
AGO learning rate: the model with the better SFT F1 is the Guide with the lower LR (5e-6); the worse one is the Learner with the higher LR (1e-5).

AGO temperature: set by parameter size only; the larger model gets tau=2.0 and the smaller gets tau=3.0. The gradient derivation shows an 'asymmetric shift force' proportional to (tau_rival^2 - tau_k^2).
Two regimes: Reshaping (small learner / large guide) and Extraction (large learner / small guide).

setting.training_data: SNEI (265/60 train/test scenarios, 1,625 image-text pairs) and MUSON (640/160 scenarios, 4,000 pairs); 10 epochs, cosine LR, 8x RTX8000, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3
setting.action_space: high-level text social navigation action/instruction (no low-level control)
setting.simulator: none (offline social-navigation datasets SNEI and MUSON)

numbers_note: Not a navigation-benchmark paper; results are Action-F1 and cosine similarity on the SNEI and MUSON test sets, with no simulator metrics. Only the main pairs are listed; the paper reports many more group configurations. The 'test' split label is assumed from the 'train/test' description.
results: GCL lifts SNEI Action-F1 from 0.692 to 0.968 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B (+40%) and from 0.816 to 0.914 for Qwen3-VL-4B (+12%). The GCL-trained 3B model beats the SFT 8B baseline (0.755) and the SFT 4B baseline. All 12 groups on SNEI and 12 on MUSON improve over SFT, and the best guide reaches 0.988.
limitations: No real-robot or closed-loop navigation experiments; evaluation is offline text-based Action-F1 and embedding similarity only.

Hyperparameters (tau 2/3, LR ratio, loss weights) need calibrating to the capability gap and are sensitive: a large LR ratio or DRL weight collapses the guide. Only Qwen family models were tested, and the SFT baselines were not tuned exhaustively.
Failure cases remain in fine-grained spatiotemporal reasoning, e.g. reflective surfaces and human-object interaction at doors.
builds_on: Online knowledge distillation / deep mutual learning
